Field Compendium

shift 102462 classified28 still living407 with measurements11 categories

A record of everything that has lived in this terrain and been looked at closely.

Each drawing is made from that specimen's own measurements — how much it carried, how far it reached, how many others it could hold on to, how long it lasted. Nothing is drawn from imagination, and no two look alike because no two sets of numbers are alike.

The groupings are not ours either. A classifying agent called the Namer watches what each specimen does, decides for itself what kinds of thing are here, and names them. Its words appear below exactly as it wrote them — they are the finding, not a summary of one.

Each entry opens with a plain description. Those sentences are built by fixed rules from the specimen's own measurements — the same numbers the drawing uses — so they describe what was recorded and never guess. They say what a specimen was like and how it made its living; they never say what KIND of thing it was. That judgement belongs to the Namer, and its word for it is the heading above each group.

Where a specimen shows an empty frame, it died before this terrain began keeping remains, and nothing survives to draw from.

How to read an entry

Every figure below is a measurement the terrain recorded. None of them have units — they only mean something next to each other, so each one is also described in plain words against every other specimen on record.

reach
How far out it can gather light from the ground around it. A long reach collects from a wider area but costs more to keep up.
holds N links
How many other specimens it can be joined to at once. Light moves along those joins — sometimes given, sometimes taken.
carries
How much substance it has. More lets it store more light and resist having light pulled off it by others, and costs more every shift to hold together.
makes its living by
Where its light actually comes from. ground is the cover layer growing where it stands; remains is what dead specimens left behind; others is light drawn along links from other living things.
upkeep
What it must spend every shift simply to keep existing. If it cannot cover this, it dies. Everything else has to be earned on top of it.
can hold
The most light it can store at once. Anything beyond this is lost.
lasted
How many shifts it was alive. A shift is one tick of the terrain.

The drawing is built from those same numbers: the core is what it carries, the spokes are its links, their length is its reach, the rings are offspring, and the disc beneath is how much it lived off remains.

why the Namer grouped it here

i-13265 exhibits a distinct behavioral profile that warrants a new category. It meets the movement threshold for mobile_exchanger (10 moves across 12 shifts), but differs in resource strategy and reproductive output. Key distinctions: (1) Residue intake at 30% is substantially higher than typical mobile_exchangers (observed range 0–37%, but clustering in 0–12% for recent cohort); this elevation-0.74 position and residue-inclusive strategy suggest active foraging in residue-accumulation zones. (2) Zero link-derived intake (0%) despite active transfer (0.74 light passed / 52.83 total taken = 1.40% outflow) indicates unidirectional redistribution similar to anomalous i-03417, but with younger tenure and lower complexity. (3) Moderate complexity (12) is at the lower end of mobile_exchanger range but above static_accumulator typical ceiling. (4) Only 2 descendants—reproductive output lower than age-matched mobile_exchangers. This specimen appears to be a young mobile organism developing a residue-specialized foraging strategy, potentially a proto-mobile_exchanger or a distinct 'residue_forager' type. Its 10-event movement pattern and sustained transfer suggest it is not a static_accumulator, but its residue dependence and zero reciprocal intake mark it as distinct from the established mobile_exchanger cohort.

i-03985 shows 4 discrete movement events over 19-shift tenure. While this sits at the boundary between episodic (1–3 events) and sustained (3+ events), the movement pattern is sparse relative to tenure length—roughly one move per 5 shifts, far lower density than mobile_exchanger specimens (which move once per 1.5–2 shifts). The movement count alone does not trigger sustained classification; movement frequency matters. Outward transfer is 3.72 / 56.92 = 6.5% of intake, which exceeds the mobile_exchanger floor (> 2%), but this high transfer coupled to low movement frequency and zero offspring suggests a different behavioral profile: the specimen is repositioning opportunistically and shedding resources rather than maintaining a mobile lifestyle. Resource strategy is heavily residue-dominant (57% residue, 43% cover, 0% links), which is atypical for mobile_exchanger (which averages 10–37% residue) and uncommon for static_accumulator. This residue-focused intake combined with low-frequency moves places i-03985 in episodic_relocator: it moves when residue opportunities emerge, harvests residue pools, and transfers some acquire to others, but does not establish a systematic mobile routine.
